blindSummary: In May 2025 the state's municipal authority installed warning signboards about homosexual practice at several strategic locations, framing homosexuality as 'dirty'; when criticised, a state executive-council member confirmed the aim was deliberate — the boards were meant 'to instil hatred towards such acts among the community.' The national trans-rights monitoring group and twelve other civil-society organisations demanded removal on 14 May 2025 as a human-rights violation, so the record combines an explicit official statement of hostile intent with a documented civil-society counterweight. This state/province additionally maintains a 2002 religious-statutory enactment that is unenforceable because of the federal penalty cap — an aspirational religious-law ceiling the unit nonetheless keeps legislating on, having amended its discretionary-penalty provisions from December 2022. What a visitor encounters is visible, ongoing, official hostility: signboards at strategic locations broadcasting that the state's stated purpose is to generate hatred; there is no criminalisation of trans status per se (in contrast to a neighbouring state/province), and the hostility is explicit and official rather than atmospheric.
blindSourceSummaries: A national newspaper (10 May 2025): a state executive-council member defends anti-homosexuality warning signboards — installed near the state university and other youth-frequented areas deliberately as a 'constant reminder' — confirming the purpose is to educate away from homosexuality; a transgender activist condemns the move as institutionalised discrimination.

A national newspaper (14 May 2025): the national trans-rights monitoring group and 12 other civil-society organisations urge the state capital's city council to immediately remove the anti-LGBT signboards, calling them discriminatory hate speech under international human-rights law and condemning the executive member's defence as inciting hatred.

A faith-based rights group's analysis (June 2023) of the state/province's religious criminal-offences framework: the 2001 discretionary-penalty enactment, its December 2022 amendments, and the 2002 corporal-punishment enactment that is rendered unenforceable by the federal penalty ceiling — the documentary basis for the unit's shadow capital-punishment code.
